morph.stmt: Machoni describes a language whose grammatical marking is added at the end of the word or postposed: nouns are 'indeclinables' but case relations use 'partículas [que] se posponen al nombre' (lé, má, tá, yá; 'la preposición siempre se pospone', cap. IX §XII), possessor and subject person, tense, subjunctive lé, imperative, interrogative má/yá and prohibitive tò are all formed 'añadiéndoles las partículas' after the root (caps. III-V, VIII), and even ornamental particles 'casi siempre se posponen' (cap. VII); the 2sg imperative is the bare stem ('no se añade partícula, sino que se les quita alguna letra, ó una se muda en otra', cap. IV-V). The only preposed bound material is derivational…

1339.dq: This first paragraph establishes some general facts of the Lumun tonal system: its tonemes, the tone-bearing unit, and the distribution of tones.
1339.dloc: ch. 3 Tone, §3.1.1 'Four tonemes', pp. 81-82; §3.1.2 (mora as TBU) pp. 83-84; ch. 4 §4.2 'Tone patterns' p. 123 (Arabic loans)
1339.prule: Tone language: four contrastive tonemes (H, L, HL, LH) realized on the mora; lexical and grammatical tone with tone rules (Tone Shift, Contour Simplification, tone bridge). No word-stress rule is described anywhere in the grammar; the only mention of 'stress' is that initial H in Arabic loans mimics the Arabic stress position.

1339.tone: Smits analyses Lumun as a tone language with four tonemes contrastive prepausally (minimal pairs given), mora as TBU, noun tone patterns L*.L, L*.H, L*.HL, L*.LH etc. The word 'stress' occurs once in the 700+ page grammar (p. 123): initial H on Arabic loans 'mimics the stress placement in the Arabic item'. No stress or accent system is posited for native vocabulary; 'accent' appears only as the name of diacritics.

1340.dq: That is, main stress is assigned to the first syllable of the root (skipping over any prefixes), and every other syllable thereafter receives secondary stress.

1340.prule: Main stress on the (first syllable) root; prefixes/proclitics unstressed (extrametrical); Cable 2009 adds trochaic L-to-R feet from the root giving alternating secondary stress; stressed root vowel typically lengthened. Position is fixed relative to the root, not the word edge. Hedges: Tucker (via Swenson) 'mainly falls on the root vowel'; Gregersen 1961 (via SPA 1979) calls stress 'unpredictable' in polysyllabic utterances on purely phonological grounds while noting the root syllable is 'usually the stressed syllable'.
1340.srule: Secondary stress on every other syllable after the root-initial main stress (trochaic feet, left to right from the root), stated only by Cable 2009 (course handout, hedged 'seems to be relatively straightforward'); no primary description opened (Tucker 1994 via Downing 2004, Swenson 2015, Owino 2003, Oduor 2002/2017) mentions alternating secondary stress.

1340.tone: Dholuo is a tone language: Cable 2009 sec. 4.3 "Like many languages of Africa, Dholuo is a tone language. There are four 'tones' or 'tonal melodies' that a vowel in Dholuo can bear: High, Low, Falling, Rising" (after Tucker 1994, who adds allotones). Stress coexists with tone; Cable notes "H-tone is not very high, especially when unstressed. (Tucker 1994: 46)". tn.quote: Like many languages of Africa, Dholuo is a tone language. There are four ‘tones’ or ‘tonal melodies’ that a vowel in Dholuo can bear: (6) The Tonal Melodies of Dholuo ... a. High: / mó̘n / món ‘women’ b. Low: / lù̘m / lum 'grass' c. Falling: / ɲâ̙ɲâ̙ / .nyânyâ 'tomato' d. Rising: / lǎ̘w / lǎw 'dress' Note that tones in Dholuo are represented just as they are in IPA, except that a low tone is indicated by the absence of any tonal diacritic. tn.translation: Prosody comprises stress ('accent tonique'), predictable and therefore non-distinctive, and tonal height (pitch), distinctive in the nominal lexicon and playing a distinctive role in verbal morphology. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable in the nominal system, whereas it is the word ... in the verbal system ... The pitches we have identified as distinctive are the high and low tones (ex 81), the mid tone being a variant of the high tone ... we will therefore maintain two distinctive tones.

1348.prule: Primary stress (= highest-pitch syllable) generally on the penultimate syllable of the word; secondary stress on every second syllable counting leftward from the primary. tn.quote: Los tres niveles de tono son alto, medio y bajo; se abrevian a, m, b, y se simbolizan en la forma á, ā, a̱. Cada vocal se pronuncia con uno de estos tonos. No hay deslices de un tono a otro en una sola vocal en las formas básicas de las palabras. Las palabras del mixteco tienen un núcleo de dos sílabas con el acento prosódico en la primera. ... Cuando una de estas palabras se pronuncia en forma aislada, hay ocho combinaciones; de las nueve posibles combinaciones, todas pueden presentarse excepto bajo bajo.
tn.translation: The three tone levels are high, mid and low; they are abbreviated a, m, b, and symbolized as á, ā, a̱. Each vowel is pronounced with one of these tones. There are no glides from one tone to another on a single vowel in the basic forms of words. Mixtec words have a nucleus of two syllables with the prosodic accent (stress) on the first. ... When one of these words is pronounced in isolation there are eight combinations; of the nine possible combinations, all can occur except low low.
tn.cite: Hollenbach, Elena Erickson de. 2004 [mayo 2004]. Los tonos del mixteco de Magdalena Peñasco. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. (SIL-Mexico electronic publication G030-TonosMixtecoMP), 47 pp.

tn.note: Three level tones (high, mid, low), one per vowel; 8 couplet patterns (no low-low), 18 counting three floating tones and a covert weak high. Progressive sandhi. Stress on couplet-initial syllable.

1352.prule: Weight-sensitive iambic-type metrical alternation (Eastern Algonquian 'vowel weakening'): a syllable is metrically strong if it has a long vowel; a short-vowel syllable is strong only if (a) lexically marked strong, (b) preceded by a weak syllable, or (c) word-final; all other short-vowel syllables are weak (their vowels reduce to extrashort or syncopate). Open and closed short syllables are treated alike. The locus of MAIN word stress among the strong syllables is not stated.
1352.srule: No separate secondary-stress rule: Goddard 2008 states one unranked metrical strong/weak grid (every long-vowel syllable strong; within runs of short-vowel syllables weak-strong alternation from the left, a short syllable being strong iff the preceding one is weak or it is lexically marked; word-final syllable always strong), so a word may have several strong syllables; which one bears main stress, and whether the others surface as secondary stresses, is not stated.

evidence_works.detail: Ten months' field research (1973-4) on Batticaloa Portuguese; derives predictable stress from phonemic vowel length via alternations such as /mi:d+a/ [mi:da] 'measure' N, /mi:d+i:/ [midi(:)] 'measure' V, /mi:d+i:+do:r/ [midido(:)r] (derivation (432), p. 76). Deciding statement p. 67: 'Having established the phonemic status of vowel length, we are now in a position to predict stress placement: stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first vowel of a word having no long vowel.' Recapitulation p. 75: 'It has been shown that vowel length must be part of the phonological representation of a word and that stress is predictable. We have formulated three rules: a Main Stress Rule, which places stress on the last long vowel of a word, a rule of Length Loss, whereby all unstressed underlying long vowels become surface short vowels, and a scalar rule of Length Adjustment, whereby stressed long vowels in non-initial syllables are reduced in length.' Fn. 18 p. 67: certain clitics and particles are never stressed and are excluded from the rule.

1363.dq: Contrastive primary word stress /´/ has been noted falling on the ultimate and penultimate syllables
1363.dloc: sec. 1.4 'Stress' and sec. 1.5 'Practical orthography' item (2), p. 25 (of 4 of archive.org)
1363.prule: Contrastive (lexical) primary word stress on either the ultimate or the penultimate syllable, shown by minimal pairs baháw/báhaw, toqód/tóqod, sabét/sábet; no default or predictive rule stated. The practical orthography leaves penultimate stress unmarked and writes ultimate stress with an acute (circumflex when it coincides with the grave marking final glottal stop), a spelling economy that hints penult is the commoner position but is not stated as a phonological rule.
1363.srule: Stated only for reduplicated roots: when a reduplicated root is pronounced as one stress group, primary stress falls on the penult of the whole form and a secondary stress on the syllable immediately before it (nakapanàwpánaw 'able to walk about a little', banìgbánig 'small mat'). The source says nothing about secondary stress in non-reduplicated words.

1364.dloc: Hildebrandt 2004, ch. 2 'Manange phonetics and phonology', section 2.6 'Word structure and stress assignment in Manange', pp. 37-39 (TOC lists p. 38); tone: section 2.5 'Tone in Manange', p. 31ff.; cross-reference in ch. 3 (case clitics: 'case markers never receive primary stress... refer back to section 2.6').
1364.prule: Non-contrastive, slight word stress 'most often' on the initial syllable of the root, explicitly quantity-insensitive ('regardless of the overall phonotactic structure of the phonological word'). Bound morphemes after the root do not take it: the grammar states outright that 'case markers never receive primary stress' (ch. 3) and shows root stress before the plural =tse, locative and the -tse converb in exx. (2.70). Manange bound morphology is suffixal/enclitic apart from the negative prefix a-, so root-initial = word-initial for nouns and non-negated verbs. Correlates: somewhat longer vowel and ~2 dB higher amplitude on the initial syllable.
1364.srule: Not stated: the grammar speaks only of 'main'/'primary' stress and describes no secondary or rhythmic stress. (The 18 final-stress disyllables of ex. 2.71 are exceptions to primary placement, recorded under exceptions, not secondary stresses.)

1364.tone: Manange is a four-tone WORD-TONE language (Tamangic/TGTM). Hildebrandt 2004 section 2.5: 'Manange has four tones, and these tones are found on all syllable types. In multisyllabics, the tone (including both pitch characteristics and segmental features of that tone) manifests itself on the first syllable of the word, and carries across the entire word... Bound grammatical morphemes are inherently toneless... the domain of tone in Manange and other Tamangic languages is not the syllable... but is rather the phonologjcal word (the root plus all bound morphemes).' Hildebrandt 2005 (LTBA): 'The domain of the tone bearing unit in Manange is the phonological word.' Stress is described separately from tone as non-contrastive and slight; tones /3/ vs /4/ additionally split by onset aspiration.
